lessons.title: parlare — "to speak," the model -are verb
lessons.gloss: to speak / to talk (your first regular -are verb)

segments.text: Until now you've assembled fixed phrases. parlare ("to speak") is your first real verb and the model for Italian's largest -are family. Learn this pattern and you drive thousands.
r-tap — a single tapped r: parlare = par-LA-reh.
vowel-a-open — clean open ah vowels.
parlare comes from Late Latin parabolāre, "to tell parables, to discourse" — from parabola, "a comparison, a speech" (Greek parabolē). So to speak is, at root, to tell parables. The English family:
parable, parole (a word of honour), palaver, parley, parliament (a talking-place).

And a lovely cross-link: Italian parlare and French parler are the same word — both from parabolāre. Spanish went a different way: its "to speak," hablar, is from fabulārī ("to chat," from fābula becomes fable). So Italy and France "tell parables"; Spain "tells fables."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the -are present tense (and pro-drop)

segments.text: Drop -are to get parl-, then add the endings:

utterances: person: (io). ending: -o. parlare, which gives:: parlo (I speak).
person: (tu). ending: -i. parlare, which gives:: parli (you speak).
person: (lui/lei). ending: -a. parlare, which gives:: parla (he/she speaks).
person: (noi). ending: -iamo. parlare, which gives:: parliamo.
person: (voi). ending: -ate. parlare, which gives:: parlate.
person: (loro). ending: -ano. parlare, which gives:: parlano.

segments.text: Like Spanish (hablo/hablas), Italian drops the subject pronoun — parlo already says "I," so you don't need io. This closes a neat circle you've been building:
Drop the pronoun: Spanish (hablo), Italian (parlo) — endings are distinct.
Keep the pronoun: French (je parle — endings silent), German (ich wohne — grammar needs a subject).

segments.instruction: parlare / parler (same parabolāre) vs Spanish hablar (fabulārī)

segments.text: What Latin word gives parlare, and which French verb is its twin? (parabolāre — French parler.) Which Romance "speak" verb is from a different root, and which? (Spanish hablar from fabulārī.) Does Italian keep or drop io, and why? (Drops it — the endings are distinct.) Next: abitare, "to live."

lessons.title: abitare — "to live," about having a place
lessons.gloss: to live / to dwell (a second -are verb — same pattern)

segments.text: A second -are verb — snap it into the endings you just learned. abitare ("to live, to dwell") lets you say where you live — and it's the twin of French habiter.
abitare = a-bee-TA-reh (Italian dropped the Latin h-, but the spelling and sense stayed). Clean open vowels, tapped r.
abitare comes from Latin habitāre, "to dwell, to keep having [a place]" — the frequentative of habēre, "to have." To dwell is to keep having your place. The English family:
habitat — where a creature dwells; inhabit, inhabitant, habitation.
via habēre ("have"): habit (what you keep having), able, ability.
French kept the h in spelling (habiter); Italian dropped it (abitare) — same Latin verb, same meaning. Now you can answer a dove ("where") question:
Abito a Roma. — "I live in Rome." (No io — pro-drop.)
Identical to parlare — nothing new. That's the whole point of a regular pattern.

segments.instruction: "Abito a Roma"; and "abitare" corresponds to English habitat

lessons.title: lavorare — "to work," the honest kind
lessons.gloss: to work (a third -are verb — and the "labour" road, not the "torture" one)

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The word, taken apart until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: A third -are verb — and a satisfying twist. Where Spanish and French built their word for "work" out of torture, Italian took a different road entirely: lavorare, from plain Latin "to labour."
lavorare = la-vo-RA-reh: clean vowels, tapped r. (The v is a real v, unlike Spanish.)
lavorare comes from Latin labōrāre, "to labour, to work, to strive" — from labor, "toil, effort." No torture device here; just honest labour. The English family is large and dignified:
labor / labour, laborious, laboratory (a working-place).
elaborate ("worked out"), collaborate ("labour together").
Here's the cross-language payoff — the same idea, two very different roots:

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 3 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: language, "to work", from, literal picture. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Spain and France remember work as torture ( becomes travail/travel); Italy remembers it as labour. A single glance at three verbs, and you see two Roman attitudes to a day's work.
Lavoro a Milano. — "I work in Milan."

segments.instruction: Italian lavorare (labour) vs Spanish trabajar / French travailler (torture)

segments.text: What Latin word is lavorare from, and its English cousins? (labōrāre — labor, laboratory, elaborate.) How does its root differ from Spanish trabajar and French travailler? (Those are from tripalium, "torture"; Italian is from labor, "toil.") Say "I work in Milan." (Lavoro a Milano.) Next: your first sentence — Parlo italiano.

lessons.title: Parlo italiano — your first real sentence
lessons.gloss: "I speak Italian" — your first full sentence (italiano = Italian)

segments.text: The moment it pays off: you take a verb you conjugated and a noun, and build a sentence no one handed you — Parlo italiano, "I speak Italian." (Italian parlo covers both "I speak" and "I am speaking.")

italiano = "Italian," from Italia — the ancient name of the peninsula itself. Its own origin is delightfully humble: many scholars trace Italia to Oscan víteliú, "land of calves / young cattle" (kin to Latin vitulus, "calf," and perhaps English veal). So Italia may literally have meant "Calf-land." Say it ee-ta-LYA-no.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the assembled sentence

segments.text: Snap two things you own together:
Parlo (I speak, from parlare) + italiano (Italian) = Parlo italiano.
A complete, grammatical Italian sentence. Notice what's not there:
No io. Italian drops it (like Spanish hablo español) — the -o of parlo already says "I". Io parlo italiano is fine for emphasis only.
No article on the language: parlo italiano.
This closes the pronoun-rule circle you've watched across five languages:

utterances: Spanish / Italian. pronoun: dropped. why: hablo/parlo: distinct endings.
French je parle. pronoun: kept. why: endings are silent.
German ich lerne. pronoun: kept. why: grammar needs an overt subject.

segments.text: Swap the pieces: Abito a Roma., Lavoro a Milano., Parli italiano?

lessons.title: Practice — making sentences with -are verbs
lessons.gloss: making sentences with -are verbs, and the pro-drop circle

segments.text: For the first time you're building Italian sentences from a pattern, not reciting phrases. Drill the three verbs until the endings are automatic — and remember, Italian drops the io.
Run each through io / tu / lui-lei (pronoun dropped in speech):
parlare: parlo, parli, parla.
abitare: abito, abiti, abita.
lavorare: lavoro, lavori, lavora.
Same endings every time (-o / -i / -a), and no pronoun needed.
— Parli italiano? — Sì, parlo un po'. E tu? — Anch'io. Dove abiti? — Abito a Roma, e lavoro a Milano. — Grazie! — Prego.
the regular -are present tense — drop -are, add -o/-i/-a/-iamo/-ate/-ano; the pronoun is dropped (like Spanish).

parlare ( from parabolāre becomes parable; = French parler, vs Spanish hablar), abitare ( from habitāre becomes habitat; twin of habiter), lavorare ( from labōrāre becomes labor/laboratory — the "labour" road, not Spanish/French "torture").
Parlo italiano — first self-assembled sentence (italiano from Italia, perhaps "calf-land").
The pronoun circle across 5 languages: ES hablo + IT parlo drop; FR je parle (silent endings) + DE ich lerne (grammar) keep.
